To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CaV1.2 and CaV1.4 Ca2+ channels co‐localize to the cell pre‐ and post‐synaptic sites, respectively, and the Ca2+ channels show elementary biophysical properties that would allow IHC synapses to generate and accurately process spontaneous Ca2+ activity characteristic of these cells

CaV1. 3 Ca2+ channel activation properties are consistent with the generation and encoding of spontaneous Ca2+ activity in immature mouse I.H.Cs and that these channels have a relatively low open probability, consistent with a low probability of neurotransmitter release.

Ca2+ channels of immature IHCs are localized at the pre‐synaptic sites and show properties that are compatible with the generation of the spontaneous activity that is characteristic of immature IHC synapses.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the localization and elementary Ca2+ currents of CaV1 channels in immature IHC synapses, and provides new information about the role of CaV1 in the generation and encoding of spontaneous activity in these cells.

the biophysical characterization of CaV1 channels in native mammalian IHCs, which is a prerequisite for understanding the role of these channels in the development and function of the auditory system.
the elementary properties of the Ca2+ channels that control synaptic transmission at IHC ribbon synaptic terminals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the elementary properties of CaV channels in native mammalian IHCs are very different from the ones found in non‐neural cells and that they are well adapted to the specific functions of these cells.
the CaV1.2 Ca2+ channels of the IHCs have properties that are well suited for their physiological roles.
CaV1.2 and CaV1.1 Ca2+ channels do not play a major role in neurotransmitter release at immature cochlear inner hair cell ribbon synapses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

CaV1.2 and CaV1.1 channels are the main Ca2+ channels involved in the regulation of neurotransmitter release from mature IHCs, whereas CaV1.4 and CaV1 channels are the Ca2+ channels responsible for the generation of Ca2+ action potentials and spontaneous release in immature cells.

Ca2+ channel function is a key factor in the generation of spontaneous EPSCs in immature IHC‐afferent nerve fibres, but that it is not a major factor in the generation and encoding of sound stimuli in adult IHC‐afferents.

immature mouse IHC synapses are endowed with a large number of CaV1‐type channels that are not fully activated by the small amplitude of Ca2+ action potentials generated by these cells, but that can generate a large number of vesicles for neurotransmitter release, which is important for the development of auditory function.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the elementary properties of CaV 1.3 Ca 2+ channels expressed by immature cochlear inner hair cell synapses are consistent with the physiological role of these channels in the generation of Ca 2+ action potential trains that drive the development of auditory nerve fibres in the mammalian cochlea.

the elementary properties of CaV 1.3 channels in IHCs are well adapted for the processing of spontaneous activity in the immature cochlea, and that the open probability, rather than the open time of these channels, may be the key determinant of the characteristic frequency/amplitudes of EPSCs recorded in auditory afferents.
IHC ribbon synapse Ca2+ channels have properties which would allow them to generate spontaneous neurotransmitter release and encode action potentials in a reliable manner during development.
